data: R-7-derived launcher for the first-generation Soyuz spacecraft — flew Soyuz 1 (1967) and Soyuz 11 (1971)

The Soyuz 11A511 was the R-7 derivative built to loft the first-generation Soyuz 7K-OK spacecraft, adding a more capable upper stage to the Vostok/Voskhod launcher lineage. Three-stage liquid-propellant (LOX + kerosene), ~50 metres tall, ~308 tonnes lift-off mass. It carried the crewed Soyuz programme's earliest flights, including its two fatal missions — Soyuz 1 (1967), lost when its recovery parachutes fouled, and Soyuz 11 (1971), whose crew died of depressurisation during descent. The 11A511 was succeeded by the Soyuz-U in 1973; the same R-7 lineage still flies crews as the Soyuz-2 today. Dedicated photographs of the 11A511 are scarce, so this gallery shows its externally near-identical R-7 successors (a 1975 Soyuz-U on the pad, later Soyuz launches, and a museum vehicle) — the same three-stage configuration, differing only in detail.

The launcher that opened the Soyuz era also carried its two tragedies. The 11A511 was the next step in Korolev's R-7 lineage — the same rocket family that lofted Sputnik and Gagarin, now uprated to carry the heavier, more capable Soyuz spacecraft that would become the workhorse of Soviet and Russian human spaceflight for the next half-century. Its first crewed flight, Soyuz 1 in 1967, ended when the descent module's parachutes fouled and Vladimir Komarov was lost. Four years later, Soyuz 11 returned its crew from the world's first space station — but a valve had opened at separation, and all three men died of depressurisation before touchdown. The rocket performed; the spacecraft's early margins did not. The R-7 lineage it belonged to still flies crews today.
